title: Severity-driven stabilization protocol: targeted rollback, hotpatch branching, and selective backporting
creator: Sofia Patel
description: Purpose: Define a clear, actionable protocol for assessing severity, creating targeted hotpatch branches, performing minimal surface-area rollbacks, and deciding selective backports into LTS channels. Goal is to reduce mean time to safe stabilization while minimizing regression surface and developer toil. Scope: covers incident-to-release workflows for runtime and control-plane changes (binary + infra config), branching conventions for hotpatch and emergency fixes, automated heuristics for candidate backports, and rollout/rollback gates integrated with the Console and CI/CD pipelines. Out of scope: feature design changes that require long-term fixes (these get tracked as regular engineering work). Success criteria: 1) <30 minutes from incident sev determination to first hotpatch branch creation + test-green smoke; 2) clear decision matrix that reduces cross-team discussions for trivial backports; 3) automation to create backport PR candidates for supported LTS branches in 80% of hotpatches; 4) documented communications/playbook and owner rotation for 24/7 coverage.
severity_matrix: Severity S0 (production outage, data loss): immediate rollback to last known-good LTS or emergency hotpatch; S1 (degraded but functional, significant error rate): controlled rollback or canary hotpatch with circuit breaker gating; S2 (partial impact, low error rate): schedule hotpatch following smoke validation; S3 (no customer impact): standard sprint fix. Criteria include: customer-facing errors, SLO breaches >5% for >5 minutes, data integrity risk, and regulatory exposure.
branching_convention: Hotpatch branches: hotfix/<component>/ENG-<ticket>-<short-desc> (e.g., hotfix/runtime/ENG-52750-kv-cache-fix). Patch branches generated for backports: patch/runtime-1.22/<ticket>. Naming scheme ensures discoverability in release trackers. Hotpatch branches must target minimal files; no refactors. Merge flow: hotpatch branch -> CI smoke -> QA signoff -> merge to current release branch; then evaluate backport candidates to LTS branches.
backport_policy: Backport eligibility rules: 1) Must fix regression or SLO breach; 2) Risk assessment: code touch size < 5 files and no API contract change; 3) Automated test coverage >80% for touched modules or manual test plan attached. Automatic backport candidate PRs are created by a bot for supported LTS branches (runtime-1.22, runtime-1.21). Owners must approve or reject within 2 business days. If rejected, record reason and create follow-up issue.
rollout_gates_and_checks: Pre-merge gates: Lint, unit tests, minimal integration smoke. Post-merge rollout: canary (5% traffic) for 15 minutes with key SLOs monitored: p99 latency, error ratio, token-level anomaly. Gate automation: console rollout-stage will auto-promote if no alerts, otherwise auto-halt and notify on-call. Manual override requires two approvers and explicit rollback plan.
rollback_steps: 1) Triage and severity confirmation; 2) If rollback chosen: trigger release-rollback job targeting last-green tag and run parallel smoke and DB-migration reversion checks; 3) Post-rollback validation runbook (smoke + canary) and escalate to SE on-call if anomalies persist; 4) Open postmortem and schedule hotpatch fix job if rollback is temporary. Communication: post to #incidents, update status page, and send customer-facing note for S0/S1 incidents.
automation_tasks: - Implement bot to create backport PR candidates and label with 'backport-candidate' and target branch checks. - Add CI job 'hotpatch-smoke' that runs prioritized end-to-end smoke tests within 10 minutes. - Integrate Console alerts to block promotion and create incident link if gates fail. - Add output to release dashboard with per-hotpatch latency/cost delta.
tradeoffs_and_risks: Trade-offs: stricter backport criteria reduces regressive churn but increases time-to-fix in LTS; aggressive automated backports speed fixes but risk incorrect merges in fragile code. Risks: human error during manual rollbacks, overlooked DB schema dependencies, and cascading failures if canary metrics are insufficiently discriminative. Mitigations: mandatory runbook checklist, DB migration safety tags, and post-merge short TTL hold in canary.
